text:
Let Builders Decide How Much Parking to Build

Every city that requires a minimum number of parking spaces has made a quiet bet: that a planning department knows better than a developer, a lender and a future tenant how many cars a building will need. The bet keeps losing. Cities should remove minimum parking requirements from their planning codes, and they should do it citywide rather than one corridor at a time.

Start with cost. A parking space is never free. Structured spaces often cost tens of thousands of dollars each to build, and surface lots consume land that could hold homes or shops. When a code requires 1.5 spaces per apartment, that cost is folded into the rent whether or not a tenant owns a car. Donald Shoup, the UCLA planner who spent decades studying this question, argued that minimums effectively subsidize driving at the expense of everyone who doesn't drive. The renter who bikes to work pays for the garage under the building next door. That is a regressive transfer, and it lands hardest on the households least likely to own two cars.

Second, the requirements don't track reality. They are usually drawn from generic national tables of parking demand, applied uniformly across neighborhoods that differ enormously in transit access, household size and car ownership. A studio a block from a subway station and a large house at the edge of a bus-free suburb get the same arithmetic. Developers who know their market will build what their tenants need. A minimum forces them to build more when they don't need it, and it offers no help where spillover is real. Where a building does need parking, the market will supply it, because tenants who need a space will pay for one.

Third, minimums work against the housing supply cities say they want. Parking consumes the lot. On small infill sites, required spaces can make a project financially impossible, so the parcel stays a parking lot or becomes one more single-family house. Cities that have removed minimums have seen construction on marginal parcels that were previously uneconomic, including small apartment buildings and conversions. Buffalo eliminated citywide minimums in 2017 as part of a broader zoning overhaul, Hartford followed in 2018, and Minneapolis did so in 2021 with the explicit goal of lowering the cost of new homes. Developers in these cities have generally kept building some parking, but fewer spaces, sized to what their buyers and renters actually want. That is the outcome a functioning market should produce.

Fourth, the climate and safety case. Parking lots add impervious surface, retain heat and send stormwater runoff into drains. Every space that isn't mandated is a space that doesn't have to be paved, and every household that chooses not to own a car is one fewer car on the street. The people most likely to live in car-light buildings are often the ones who gain most from walkable blocks, including older residents, young people and those who cannot afford a second vehicle.

The objections deserve direct answers. The strongest is spillover. A new building with no parking can push residents' cars onto neighboring streets, and existing residents notice. The answer is to manage the curb itself: residential permit parking, metered on-street spaces priced to keep a few spots open, and consistent enforcement. It is not to require every new building to subsidize free storage for private cars on public land.

Second, accessibility. Removing minimums must not remove accessible parking. Residents with disabilities need dependable spaces close to their doors, and a code can keep a specific accessibility requirement while dropping general counts. Third, lenders and insurers sometimes want parking on site. That is a reason for a developer to provide it voluntarily, not a reason for the city to mandate it for everyone.

Cities should go further. They can cap parking in transit-rich areas, unbundle spaces from rent so that residents can choose whether to pay for one, and invest in the transit, sidewalks and bike lanes that make car-light life practical. But the first step is simple: delete the minimum. Let the people who finance, build and live in these buildings decide how much parking they need, and let the cost of that decision fall on the people who make it.
